Episcoporum acceptarent; at non hanc, fed aliam, cum variis nempe restrictionibus, distinctionibus sensuum, exposcebat Cavalerius. Ad extremum deposita omni verecundia per Tremoillium varia postulata Papæ ab opponentibus exposita, & inter hæc Concilium nationale, a quo, ut appellatio ad Generale fieri posset, pro fundamento stabilire ausi sunt. Verum Clemens, his tricis, & fraudibus ut finem imponeret, paucis respondit: duas superesse vias finiendæ compositionis, spontaneam submissionem, vel vim Canonicam. Sicque terminata fuit Cavalerii negotiatio.

§. 4.
*Appellatio ad Concilium Generale.*

Vaticana jam parabantur fulmina: Noaillius ab ipso Cardinalium Collegio purpura indignus censebatur. Nihilominus datum tempus adhuc resipiscendi, ex spe, quam ostenderant Opponentes confecto quodam doctrinæ schemate, quod cum ab acceptantibus probatum non fuit, scriptum eis trium columnarum, Janseniano illi olim simile obtulerunt, in quarum media ipsæ propositiones Quesnelli, ex una parte sensus obvius, ex altera alius quispiam Catholicus, vel certe excusationis patiens

patiens legebatur. Sed nec istud placere potuit, additæque ab acceptantibus glossæ, quibus ostendebant, & sensum obvium propositionum recte damnatum, & alterum eas, nisi per violentam detorsionem habere non posse. Ne tamen una cum hoc negotio spes omnis iterum intercideret, Cardinalis Rohanus Aurelianensem permovit, ut ad 20. Nov. 1716. conventum Episcoporum indiceret, in quo Acceptantes aliquam explicationem Bullæ proponerent. Id ægerrime tulit Pontifex, & omni modo hoc consilium impedire aggressus, duo Brevia misit, unum Duci, quid Noaillio pararet, significans, alterum Sorbonæ, cui facultates & omnia privilegia ad tempus suspendit: cumque Tremoillius Cardinalibus, qui alias literas cum amicissimis hortatibus ad Noaillium dederant, & Papæ ipsi persuadere vellet, ut quidpiam de danda vel admittenda quadam explicatione adderetur; hic tertium Breve adjecit ad Episcopos acceptantes, quo eos hortatus est, ne se ab Opponentibus decipi sinant, & neque ullam a se Bullæ explicationem expectarent, nec ipsimet darent, aut admitterent. Verum Aurelianensis Cardinalium literas Noaillio non exhibuit, qui interea Parlamento Duacensi, quod Theses quasdam Constitutioni faventes suppressisset…

§. 4.
*Appeal to a General Council.*

The thunders of the Vatican were now being prepared; Noailles was judged by the College of Cardinals itself to be unworthy of the purple. Nevertheless, time was still given to repent, from the hope that the Opponents had shown by having completed a certain scheme of doctrine, which, when it was not approved by those accepting, they offered them a writing of three columns, similar to that Jansenist one of old, in the middle column of which were the propositions of Quesnell themselves, on one side the obvious sense, on the other some other Catholic one, or at least one capable of excuse

it was read with patience. But neither could this satisfy, and glosses were added by those accepting the bull , by which they demonstrated that the obvious sense of the propositions had been rightly condemned, and that they could possess no other meaning unless through a violent distortion. Yet, lest every hope perish once more along with this matter, Cardinal Rohan persuaded the Bishop of Orléans to convene an assembly of Bishops on November 20, 1716, in which the Acceptantes might propose some explanation of the Bull. The Pontiff took this very ill, and having attempted in every way to impede this plan, he sent two Briefs : one to the Duke, signifying what he was preparing against Noailles, and another to the Sorbonne, for which he suspended its faculties and all privileges for a time. And when La Trémoille wished to persuade the Cardinals, who had otherwise given letters with the most friendly exhortations to Noailles, and the Pope himself, that something should be added regarding the giving or admitting of a certain explanation, the latter added a third Brief to the accepting Bishops, in which he urged them not to allow themselves to be deceived by the Opponents, and neither to…

…rious restrictions and distinctions of senses, that Cavalier demanded. At last, having laid aside all shame, various demands of the Pope were exposed by the opponents through Trémoille, and among these a national Council, from which, so that an appeal to a General one could be made, they dared to establish as a foundation. But Clement, so that he might put an end to these trickeries and frauds, replied in few words: there remained two ways of finishing the composition, spontaneous submission or Canonical force. And thus the negotiation of Cavalier was terminated.

It is understood that they have not yet departed from that port for fear of the storm, and they will make the journey to us as soon as that storm subsides. May our messages result in good fortune. I wished for these things to be known to you primarily through our triremes, so that you might be better informed about all your affairs and might set aside all anxiety, if perhaps you have conceived any from this shipwreck. Since you are a prudent man in all other matters, there is nothing for which I need to admonish you. For you can judge for yourself that the goods are worth much more, even had there been no shipwreck. I will expedite the rest when the time comes. If you wish for me to do anything else regarding your affairs, please signify it to me by your letters. Farewell.

 Nothing could be added to this anxiety of yours. You have acted so that even if all things had gone to ruin, I would still have been grateful to you, since your business could not have been conducted with greater zeal than that with which you have conducted my affairs at this time.

———— page break ————

I am, however, extremely joyful and give many thanks that fortune has favored your diligence. For when I had poured so much of my money into those goods, and I had never before exhausted my funds for the sake of trading, I saw almost all my fortune as having been committed to the winds. But by divine favor, that ship of ours, along with the other funds, has safely reached port. Your letters were all the more welcome to me because I was hoping for less regarding the safety of our affairs. Already, a short time before I received them, a rumor had arisen about this shipwreck. There were those who said that no danger at all had been avoided. But as for your warning me about the scarcity of goods, so that I might be more cautious and prudent in my own affairs, you do this rightly, as you do everything else. For I will be diligent and attentive, so that when fortune has been of help to me, I do not appear to have failed myself. Regarding other matters that pertain to me, there is nothing else I need to demand from you, except that as soon as you have finished, you sail to us. For I have much to confer with you, which will bring the greatest utility (as I hope) to both of us. But see that…

…espair of your friends. I, as I say regarding myself, will see to it that in no way, while I have abundance, will I allow you to suffer from any lack of life's necessities. I judge that all who loved you for your own sake know this. Farewell.

 That I have been reduced to poverty, which I see happens to many, I bear with a mind somewhat more elevated than my fortune. But since all my studies, by doing well for many, have fallen into ruin, I cannot be sufficiently satisfied. How could I have been led to the point where I would be treated poorly by those for whom I have been thrifty and liberal? You know well enough what benefits and services our fellow citizens have received from me. How ungrateful they have been toward me, time itself has taught. For when those men whom I had made my friends for the sake of our common salvation had turned against me, and had instigated judges and prepared false witnesses against me, who was there to defend my rights? Or who was willing to protect my dignity? But I feel that it happens with good reason that I experience them as ungrateful, in whose love for me there was no rationale. For I know and understand that what is in the old proverb is true.

———— page break ————

It is no new thing you write to me, nor is it unknown to me. For how often have you believed that I, by the indignity of such fortune, have frequently seen myself and other citizens, both honest and distinguished, endure things beyond what is good and fair? Although this calamity of ours is nothing compared to yours, it happens nevertheless (I know not how) that we feel less burdened by the troubles that are common in the city. I would prefer, however, that you seek aid for this distress from your own wisdom rather than from common habit. For I know this will be the result: that nothing will more alleviate your grief than the realization that none of these things happened to you because of your own merit. And your opinion, as it is now, will change greatly if you take more account of your own virtues than of the distress that is still fresh. You write to me, not for the sake of aid or counsel in a desperate matter, but because it helps you to speak with me about your troubles. You do what is customary among friends. I am accustomed to doing the same. I know that I am unburdened in spirit when I have revealed my every distress to my friends. For this, I am most grateful, and I thank…

For he does not understand that that bread and that wine (which are offered to them as sacraments of the body and blood of Christ) are also called the body and blood by Christ. While he does not understand this, he strips the sun of its light, that is, he strips the very flesh of Christ of its life-giving power. But hear now what the arguments of this man are.

Christ in the Holy Supper offered the same thing to be eaten and drunk by all, that is, the same thing to Judas Iscariot and to John the Evangelist. Therefore, Judas Iscariot received the same thing that John the Evangelist did, albeit with unequal fruit; Judas, to be sure, to his destruction, but John to his salvation. 

Response: This sun offers its light to the blind, yet the blind do not see or enjoy that light. For just as the sight of the eyes is the only instrument for enjoying the light of the sun, so faith is the only mouth

———— page break ————

and the instrument for eating the true flesh and blood of Christ. For it is not food for the belly but for the mind: it is not taken by the mouth but by faith, and spiritual things require spiritual instruments. Therefore, what is said by that man, that Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, took and ate the body of Christ itself, but to his own destruction, is false. For the body of Christ is altogether life-giving to anyone who eats it. How, therefore, is the flesh of Christ to anyone's destruction? It is when it is spurned, not when it is taken and eaten. For it is death when spurned, not when taken. Christ in the Holy Supper offered the same thing to all to be eaten and drunk, that is, the same to Judas Iscariot and to John the Evangelist. In this passage, Osiander cooks up and throws back at us the primary argument of the Apollinarist heretics, who attribute divinity to the flesh of Christ just as a soul is attributed to a body. Therefore, it does not conclude that he is present everywhere.

…nts and various pamphlets, two of which were accused of attacking episcopal authority or at least showing it too little deference. Sancyranus seized this opportunity to declaim against the regulars and issued that famous pamphlet on the *Hierarchy* under the pseudonym of *Petrus Aurelius*. The work was well-received as long as the author remained hidden, and it was approved by the Synod of the Gallican Clergy on April 27, 1641, and committed to the press at their expense. Antoine Godeau, Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is proclaimed an "invincible defender of bishops, a most fierce lover of the truth, a most just vindicator of the Hierarchy, and a theologian raised in the bosom of ancestral theology." Sancyranus's modesty did not have enough strength to allow him to remain hidden any longer amidst such commendation of himself and his work. But when the author was discovered, a blush covered their faces, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book *Gallia Christiana*.

Indeed, he proved himself a candidate of ancestral theology in the book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Familiar Theology, or a brief explanation of the mysteries of the Faith*

…mphlets, two of which were accused of criticizing episcopal authority, or certainly of deferring to it too little. Sancyranus seized this opportunity to declaim against the religious orders and published that famous pamphlet on the *Hierarchy* under the assumed name of *Petrus Aurelius*. The work was pleasing as long as the author remained hidden, and it was approved by the Synod of the Gallican Clergy on April 27, 1641, and committed to the press at their expense. Godeau, the Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is heralded as "the most invincible defender of Bishops, the most keen lover of truth, the most just vindicator of the Hierarchy, and a theologian raised in the bosom of ancestral theology." The modesty of Sancyranus did not have enough strength to cause him to prefer remaining hidden any longer amidst such commendation of himself and his labor. But once the author was discovered, a blush covered his face, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book *Gallia Christiana* .

Indeed, he proved himself a candidate of "ancestral theology" in the book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Theologia Familiaris, seu brevis explicatio mysteriorum Fidei*

By the joy and gladness of His ascension, deliver us, O mistress. By the joy and gladness of your coronation, deliver us, O mistress. In the hour of devastating death, deliver us, O mistress. In the strict examination of the judge, deliver us, O mistress. From the horrible torment of hell, deliver us, O mistress.

We sinners beseech you, hear us. That you may deign, most pious mistress, to preserve the holy Church, we beseech you. That you may deign to obtain glory for the just and grace for sinners, we beseech you. That you may deign to obtain consolation for the troubled and liberation for the captive, we beseech you. That you may deign to comfort your servants, both male and female, who serve you with devotion, we beseech you. That you may deign to preserve the Christian people, redeemed by the precious blood of your Son, we beseech you. That you may deign to grant eternal rest to all the faithful departed, we beseech you. Mother of God, we beseech you. Daughter of God, we beseech you. Most dear Mother, our mistress, have mercy on us and grant us perpetual peace. Amen. Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Our Father, and lead us not into temptation. But deliver us.

From this, I have said: Lady, have mercy on me. Heal my soul, because I have sinned before your face. Turn your mercy upon us and be favorable to your servants. Show your power against our enemies, that you may be justified among the nations of the peoples. Have mercy on your servants over whom your name has been called, and do not allow them to be distressed in their temptations. Look upon us in the time of our death, and assist my soul when it leaves its body. Be for us, Lady, a tower of strength and a most hard rock against the enemy. Help me, Lady, that I may not fall before him. Cause him to be crushed under my feet. Hear my prayer and my supplication, and let my adversaries be put to shame.

Almighty and everlasting God, who deigned to be born for us from the most chaste Virgin Mary, make us serve you with a chaste body and please you with a humble mind. We also pray to you, most pious Virgin Mary, Queen of the world and Lady of the angels.

Ninth, I sinned by omission, because I neglected to keep the three theological virtues and the four cardinal virtues. In me there is not true faith in Christ with good works. In me there is not certain hope regarding future heavenly goods. In me there is not charity, which loves God above all things, and I did not love my neighbor as myself. In me there is not temperance, because I refused to sustain labors, fasts, and tribulations. All good men were stunned, until Saint-André, Bossuet's Vicar, who as a witness and arbiter knew everything that had been done by the Bishop in this matter, exposed the most disgraceful frauds. Then indeed the indignation of all erupted, the work was referred to the sacred tribunals, and antidotes against the plague were sought. Meanwhile, Quesnel, having been established as the head of the faction after Arnauld, and Gerberon, having scattered seditious pamphlets throughout Belgium and Gaul as was reported above, taking occasion especially from the aforementioned case of conscience, threw everything into confusion; and by now the unbridled license of those men seemed to be restrainable only by the application of force. But this was the difficult task. Quesnel, by frequently changing his hideouts, his clothing, and his assumed names—now called Father Prior or Provincial of the Augustinians, now Monsieur de Fresne, Frekerberg, Baron de Rebeck, du Puis, etc.—had hitherto eluded the diligence of the most sagacious men.

Finally, Humbert-Guillaume de Precipiano, Archbishop of Mechelen, after he had subjected another priest of the Oratory, Van Hame, to canonical penalties in the year 1700 for spreading principles contrary to the faith despite repeated warnings, and in 1702 had initiated proceedings against Quesnel in Rome, received more certain information regarding their hiding places in the following year. In 1703, he first captured Gerberon, who was dragged from the outermost corner of the city of Brussels. Quesnel himself, along with his inseparable companion Brigode, who—although warned by Roman letters to depart the city—had only changed his lodgings by moving to the house called *Refuge de Forest* , was discovered there. Noailles was terrified all the more by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in upholding its acts. Many bishops had gathered at Embrun in the year 1727 to overthrow the immense errors that were being scattered everywhere by the schismatics and to settle the disturbances stirred up by them. Furthermore, there were two principal acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer from the monastery of Saint Genevieve along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who, intending to execute the system of Dupin , crossed over into England, and raised himself there with other writings concerning the ordinations of Anglican Bishops; and secondly, the sentence brought on September 20th against Soanen , the Bishop of Senez . A certain pastoral Instruction had appeared under his name, teeming with infamous errors of every kind, and in which, as much as the work of Quesnel was commended, so much was the Bull condemning it prostituted as if worthy of every execration. Condemning

this instruction is demanded of the Bishops; he himself is summoned to the council to give an account. Soanen, having initially prevaricated, once thirteen Bishops had been named before whom he might plead his cause—and against whom he himself had nothing to object—finally set out for Embrun, not without a profane retinue, and one that was not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to the assembled group that he would never recognize them as judges. Subsequently, when asked by the Council whether that was indeed his Instruction, he did indeed deny that he had composed it, yet nonetheless openly professed that he entirely adopted, held, and approved it as his own, until he should be convinced of the errors which the Bishops had condemned in it. Indeed, the obstinacy of this man could not be overcome. For this reason, by the sentence of the Council, he was interdicted from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese.  I give thanks to your immense majesty and eternal piety, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who has deigned to satisfy me, your unworthy servant and miserable sinner, not because my merits demand it, but by your many and great mercies, with the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let it be the evacuation of my vices, the extermination of concupiscence and lust, the augmentation of humility, charity, patience, chastity, obedience, and all virtues, as well as of all holiness and salvation. Let it be a firm defense against the snares of all my enemies, visible and invisible. Let it be the perfect quieting of all my impulses, both carnal and spiritual. Let it be a firm adherence to you, the living and true God, and a happy fulfillment of my end.

However, having changed their plans shortly thereafter, they departed for the territory of Liège and settled near a certain castle. Finding themselves less secure there, they soon entered the city itself and kept themselves there until the end of August, known to very few. When they grew weary of being tossed about, they disregarded the danger and returned secretly to Brussels after six months, seeking their old hiding places, from which, by the testimony of Quesnel himself in certain of his letters, they did not set foot for the entire four years that Arnauld survived. During this time, Quesnel polished his work, and Arnauld, with his assistance, sought to exert his final strength against the Bulls of the Popes and against the recent Decree of Alexander VIII, by which 31 propositions and many of Arnauld’s own were condemned, in a book written as *Difficulties Proposed Against Doctor Steyart of Leuven*. Having finished this labor, the old man, a bridge-jumper of 82 years, having received the viaticum from the hands of Quesnel, expired on August 8, 1694.

… ubique præfentem eodem tempore & fimul fifteret.

Filius Dei per fuam humanitatem affumptam fuas actiones & operationes efficit, vt in humano corpore anima per fuum corpus fuas actiones perficit. Ergo cum ubique operetur Filius Dei, ubique præfentem effe eius carne oportet. R. Primùm Apolinariftarum hæreticorum argumentum recoquit, ac regerit nobis hoc loco Ofiander, qui Deitatem carni Chrifti, velut animam corpori attribuit. Deinde ipfamet fimilitudo Ofiandri vbiquepræfentiam carnis Chrifti euertit. Vt enim non omnes operationes fuas Anima etiã corpori hypoftaticè vnita per corpus exercet, velut, meditari, ratiocinari, & fimilia: fic nec Deitas Chrifti perficit omnes actiones fuas per fuam humanitatem, etiam poft vnionem. Ergo vbique præfentem effe non concludit.

 Pag. 28. Humanitas à Chrifto affumpta eft vna perfona cum ipfius Deitate, & cum ea hypoftaticè eft vnita. Ergo vbicunque eft Deitas Chrifti, illic quoque eft ipfius caro feu humanitas. R. Primùm præfentiam Chrifti in Cœna Domini ifte priùs non ex vnione hypoftatica: fed ex his verbis Chrifti, Hoc eft corpus meum, fumebat. Deinde infirmum effe hoc fuum præfidium iam agnofcens illud deferit, & fe ad vnionem hypoftaticam,

vel omnipotentiam Dei recipit, quòd nullas satis sibi tutas latebras videat. Sed ex his ipsis à nobis educatur, & σοφὸν istius hominis φάρμακον iam detegamus. *Caro & Deitas in Christo hypostaticè vniuntur.* Ergo vbicunque hæc est, & illa. Eodem modo: Caput & pedes eiusdē hominis hypostaticè vniuntur ad vnius indiuidui οὐσίαν . Ergo vbi est caput istius hominis, illic quoque sunt pedes. Quis hoc concedet? Præterea cùm Deitas sit infinita, caro autē assumpta sit finita, omnino fieri non potest, vt coextendantur in persona Christi Deitas, & humanitas. Conqueruntur quasi vnam Christi personam, velut Nestorius faciebat, discerpamus. Negamus verò, nisi ipsi fortè sint Eutychiani, quoniā istā duarū in vna Christi persona naturarū vnionem hypostaticam sic factā esse dicimus, vt non modò naturæ ipsæ inconfusæ, sed etiā carū proprietates essentiales saluæ quoq; in ea vnione manserint, vt præclarè definiuit cōciliū Chalcedonēse.

…ugh its body. Therefore, since the Son of God works everywhere, his flesh must be everywhere present. Answer. Here Osiander cooks up again and casts back at us the primary argument of the Apollinarian heretics, who attribute Deity to the flesh of Christ just as a soul is attributed to a body. Furthermore, this very comparison of Osiander overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ. Noailles was terrified all the more by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in upholding its acts. Many bishops had gathered at Embrun in the year 1727 to overthrow the immense errors that were being scattered everywhere by the schismatics and to settle the disturbances stirred up by them. Furthermore, there were two principal acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer from the monastery of Saint Genevieve along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who, intending to execute the system of Dupin , crossed over into England, and raised himself there with other writings concerning the ordinations of Anglican Bishops; and secondly, the sentence brought on September 20th against Soanen , the Bishop of Senez . A certain pastoral Instruction had appeared under his name, teeming with infamous errors of every kind, and in which, as much as the work of Quesnel was commended, so much was the Bull condemning it prostituted as if worthy of every execration. Condemning

———— page break ————

this instruction is demanded of the Bishops; he himself is summoned to the council to give an account. Soanen, having initially prevaricated, once thirteen Bishops had been named before whom he might plead his cause—and against whom he himself had nothing to object—finally set out for Embrun, not without a profane retinue, and one that was not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to the assembled group that he would never recognize them as judges. Subsequently, when asked by the Council whether that was indeed his Instruction, he did indeed deny that he had composed it, yet nonetheless openly professed that he entirely adopted, held, and approved it as his own, until he should be convinced of the errors which the Bishops had condemned in it. Indeed, the obstinacy of this man could not be overcome. For this reason, by the sentence of the Council, he was interdicted from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. Furthermore, there were two principal acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer from the monastery of Saint Genevieve along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who, intending to carry out the system of Dupin , crossed over into England and exalted himself there with other writings concerning the ordinations of Anglican bishops; the other act was the sentence passed on the 20th of September against Soanen, the Bishop of Senez . Under his name, a certain pastoral Instruction had appeared, teeming with shameful errors of every kind, and by which, as much as the work of Quesnel was commended, so much was the Bull condemning it held up as if it were worthy of every execration. The condemnation

this instruction is demanded by the Bishops; he himself is summoned to the council to render an account. Soanen, having initially prevaricated, and with thirteen Bishops having been named before whom he might plead his cause, and against whom he himself had no objections, finally set out for Embrun , not without a profane escort, and one that was not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to those who had gathered that he would never recognize them as judges. Subsequently, when asked by the Council whether that Instruction was his, he indeed denied that it had been composed by him, yet nonetheless openly professed that he entirely adopted, held, and approved it as his own until he could be convinced of the errors which the Bishops had condemned within it. Indeed, the obstinacy of this man could not be overcome. Therefore, by the sentence of the Council, he was interdicted from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. ### On the seven theological and cardinal virtues.

Ninth, I sinned by omission, because I neglected to keep the three theological virtues and the four cardinal virtues. In me, there is no true faith in Christ with good works. In me, there is no certain hope for future heavenly goods. In me, there is no charity that loves God above all things, and I have not loved my neighbor as myself. In me, there is no prudence, because I did not perform my actions when and how I ought to have performed them, and I conducted my actions inconsiderately according to the desires of pleasure. In me, there is no fortitude, because I did not manfully subdue interior and exterior passions for Christ, and I did not fear to do base and shameful things. In me, there is no temperance, because I refused to sustain labors, fasts, and tribulations. In me, there is no justice, because I did not turn away from evil, but I neglected to do the good which I was bound to do, and I did not justly give to each one what was his.

———— page break ————

I gave. And because of my own benefits, I neglected the common good and the salvation of many. Therefore, whatever I have sinned against the seven virtues, I say my fault and render myself culpable.

### ¶ The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Rejecta hæc propositio fere ab omnibus, & ei a Cardinali Rohano quatuor articuli oppositi: 1. manifeste ex Bulla constare, ac tenendum esse, librum Quesnelli esse hæreticum: 2. illas 101 propositiones esse merito damnatas, & una ex subjectis censuris dignas: proinde 3. Bullam acceptari debere ante omnem ulteriorem explicationem; cum circa prædicta nec ambigua sit, nec obscura. 4. nulla alia prævia instructione opus esse, nisi qua fideles contra falsas Bullæ interpretationes præmunirentur. Saint Thomas also makes this clear in the *Summa*, Part 4, saying that the prayer he gives in the sacrament of penance restores him, if any inclination to sin should come from the circumstance of the conversation, that is, from necessary carnal speech, either in the one confessing or in the confessor. 

The seventh rule: the confessor should not look at the face of the one confessing, especially if it is a woman, so that the penitent does not blush and so that the confessor is not wounded in his soul by the feminine gaze.

———— page break ————

A stable rule: the confessor must take the greatest care that at the beginning of the confession, and especially during its progress, he is not sad, austere, or rigid, for this is very rare with penitents, whether they are timid or simple. For soon it will close the mouth of the sinner, but he should be kind and mild in the manner of a prudent physician, and affable. Therefore, before anyone begins to confess who is not accustomed to confessing—as is true of many among the bashful and the young—he may say things to open the confession, and if the matter so requires, he should ask about their homeland or children, so that whoever wishes to confess may take the courage to speak. For some people, out of bashfulness, at the beginning lose all memory of what is to be confessed, especially the young and women who rarely confess. Then he should proceed to other instructions that follow.

This is shown by the one whose place the confessor holds, Christ, when he says: "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick." Thus he himself acted, who did not abhor sinners and publicans in the city, but called them to penance; for the Son of Man came not to call the just, but sinners.

Just as our sense of things previously found pleasure in light matters, so now that those things have been disturbed and cast down, by which you long flourished among your fellow citizens, I am moved by no less a disturbance of spirit, as if everything had befallen my own affairs. For what can be called more mine than that which is yours? You have me more as a companion and participant in your hardships than as a consoler. But where there is such a power and magnitude of genius, as to be able to console yourself through letters and through my presence, you have certainly, at one and the same time, brought some aid to both of us. But I am not sufficiently capable on my own, nor have I ever been a suitable teacher for this matter. What I can easily do, that I will perform. In the first days, I will come to you, and if grief is lightened by grieving (whatever kind of consolation that may be), I will not omit anything in diminishing your grief. Meanwhile, you will borrow some counsel from letters and from philosophy, and you will be mindful that you are the same person.…

By far the greatest part of the Bishops complied, and they added the threats of canonical penalties. Hardouin de Péréfixe, elevated to the Archbishopric of Paris in the same year, was among the first to publish the mandate of subscription throughout his diocese, and in the following year, 1665, he inspects Port-Royal , both the Parisian and the one in the countryside. It is easy to divine with what sense of grief the faction saw its nest disturbed so suddenly. First there was huge trepidation, then outcries: hence the torments and mournful laments of those deploring the persecution of truth and innocence; hence the curses, devoting whatever was of sacred and profane dignity: finally, there was an uproar among the very parts of the faction, and a struggle continued for many years into the present century. Now, however, we are turning with such eagerness toward a liberty that is not feigned or shadowy (as before), but such as we received from our ancestors, that we have never lived in a truly free state if not in this time in which we now are. For those few who were oppressing the public liberty have been removed from the city, and all use equal law. It is permitted to everyone to speak about our republic and what he feels, and to feel freely what he says. The studies that they used to apply to private matters have all been turned toward the greatness of the republic. And they are most intent on this one thing: who can benefit the city the most. If, therefore, you desire to be held in high esteem among your peers, approach this republic of ours, which we have as most excellent and most beautiful. On the public utility of our citizens, and by what method that matter might be better managed by us, I have decided to write to you, so that I might open the reasoning of all my deliberations to you first. I have often perceived in my mind how the revenues and other proceeds of our city might be greatly increased without any inconvenience to our citizens or our allies. To accomplish this matter, I saw that I had need of your counsel and prudence. You are not unaware that for many years past, neither merchants nor the publicans (being moved by the fear of pirates) were able to navigate this sea of ours safely, from which it happens that our revenues have come in at a much lower amount. Since each one is led by that pact, that he perishes for himself and not for the republic, it is necessary that the profit of navigation impels them to this venture. And it happens that they do not wish to commit themselves to danger, when the greater part of the profits goes to them, from which our treasury sustains no small loss and expense. What happens to the merchants in the face of the fear of pirates is understood daily, when

Now, however, we are led with such great zeal toward a liberty that is not feigned or shadowy (as it once was), but we have received from our ancestors such that we should never live unless at this time in which we now exist. For, with the few who were oppressing public liberty removed from the city, all use equal law. It is permitted for everyone to speak about our republic and what he feels, and to feel freely what he says. The pursuits that were applied to private matters have all been turned toward the distinction of the republic. And they are especially intent on this one thing: which of them might best benefit the city. If, therefore, you desire to be considered great among your own, come to this republic of ours, which we hold to be most excellent and beautiful. You will certainly be able to do as much in it as you will provide in labor, industry, and solicitude for the rest. Farewell.

Everyone expects your presence and your duty, from which you can consider that even your enemies desire greatly to return into your favor. If you neglect this matter, you will neither consult your own reputation nor satisfy the expectation of all your fellow citizens. For the situation is such that, even if you did not have the ability, you could nevertheless persuade no one to the contrary. You must therefore work hard and apply yourself with your whole heart, so that you satisfy the will of your fellow citizens. Nothing can be better for your nature, nor more praiseworthy for your industry, than to present yourself to men and to desire those things which you understand are desired by men. For it is famously said by the Stoics that all things on earth were created for the sake of men, but men for the sake of men.

…n if a man is present, a woman may be able to baptize, not anyone’s children, but only her own. This, therefore, is our first response to this example of Zipporah. The second, however, is that he gathers a general principle from a particular instance, and establishes a perpetual rule from an extraordinary act, when we read nowhere else that women among the people of God, and under the law, circumcised their own or others' children. Moreover, this was also to the great insult and reproach of Moses himself. For the Lord, by that means, accused Moses through his wife of excessive negligence, because he had not circumcised his sons, and had neglected that sacrosanct covenant of God with his family by omitting circumcision. Finally, who does not see that the nature of Baptism and Circumcision was different in this regard? For we nowhere read that the duty of circumcision was once commanded by God specifically to the priests, since circumcision was both instituted by God and practiced by the people for more than four hundred years before the priests were separated from the rest of the people. Furthermore, Christ delegated the ministry of baptizing only to those to whom Gen. 17. Math. 28.

The second response is that he draws a general rule from a particular instance, and establishes a perpetual regulation from an extraordinary act, when we read nowhere else that women among the people of God, and under the Law, circumcised their own or others' children. Moreover, this was also done to the insult and rebuke of Moses himself. For the Lord, by that means, rebuked Moses through his wife for excessive negligence, because he had not circumcised his own sons, and had neglected that most sacred covenant of God with his family by omitting circumcision. Finally, who does not see that the nature of Baptism and Circumcision was different in this regard? ### ¶ Monday
### ¶ Nocturn

**L**ady, may the splendor of your face be my illumination: and may the serenity of your grace shine upon my mind. Lift up my head above my enemies and I will sing a psalm: I will sing a psalm to your name. Do not turn your face away from me, for I have desired your beauty and your grace since my youth. I have loved you, Queen of heaven, and I have sought your mercy: do not withdraw your grace from your servant. I will confess you among the nations: and I will honor the throne of your glory. Glory.

**U**nto you, O Lady, I will cry and you will hear me: you will gladden me with the voice of your praise. Have mercy on me in the day of my distress: and in the light of your truth, deliver me. Be blessed, O Lady, in all the ends of the earth. The sanctuary which your hands have strengthened: is the holy temple of your body. Your conscience is pure and immaculate, the place

Bring to the Lord, our Lady, children of God: bring to the Lord, our Lady, praise and reverence.
Grant strength to your servants, holy Mother: and blessing to those who praise and glorify you. Hear the sighs of those who call out to you: and do not despise the vows of those who invoke your name. Let your hand be ready to help me: and your ear attentive to my prayer. May the heavens and the earth bless you: the sea and all that the world contains.

I will exalt you, my Lady, for you have taken me up: you will free me from the wicked adversary. Turn to me and bring me to life: lead me back from the gates of death: and from the waves of tribulations that have surrounded me.

For your own sake and the magnificence of your right hand, crush and scatter all my enemies. And I will offer you a sacrifice of praise: and I will more devoutly exalt your glory. Exult, O heavens, and rejoice, O earth: for Mary consoles her people: and will have mercy on her poor.

In you, my Lady, I have hoped: I shall not be confounded forever. In your grace, receive me.

For nothing was guarded more by our ancestors than silence in deliberations concerning the matters that pertained to public utility. But enough about this to you, who are not ignorant of these things. I have written to you previously about greater matters than those I write about now, for they are such that they not only invite you to read but even demand that you be stirred to action. The greatest preparation is in motion, such as perhaps has not been seen by our city. Immense fleets are being maintained. Most well-equipped classes are being assembled. New triremes are being built. An enormous war is being prepared by land and sea against a nation that is most hostile to us. And it is the hope of all that never has a time been given to us in which we could better seize victory. If we obtain it, there will be lasting peace for our city. For the other nations, with this one exception, which could bring war upon us, have been overcome by us through love, arms, and force, and there is nothing else that remains for our commonwealth but that we also restrain this nation.
